content: Corn smut is a disease that affects maize and is caused by the pathogenic fungus Ustilago maydis. This fungus is responsible for smut disease in maize (Zea mays) and its wild ancestor, teosinte (Euchlena mexicana). While the fungus can infect any part of the maize plant, it predominantly invades the ovaries, replacing the normal kernels on the cob with large, distorted tumor-like structures. These structures, referred to as galls, consist of hypertrophied plant cells, fungal filaments, and blue-black spores. The spores give the infected cob a charred or scorched appearance, which is reflected in the etymology of the fungus's name, derived from the Latin word ustilare, meaning to burn. In the United States, corn smut is generally considered a pest because it parasitizes the corn plant, reducing crop yield. Infected crops are often destroyed. However, in Mexico, corn smut is known as huitlacoche, an Aztec term that reportedly translates to raven's excrement. Despite its unappealing name, huitlacoche is regarded as a culinary delicacy in Mexican cuisine. The galls are harvested while still immature, as fully mature galls are dry and predominantly filled with spores. Immature galls, typically collected two to three weeks after infection, retain moisture and, when cooked, are described as having a flavor profile that is mushroom-like, sweet, savory, woody, and earthy. The flavor is attributed to compounds such as sotolon, vanillin, and glucose. Efforts to introduce huitlacoche into American and European diets have faced challenges, as many farmers view it as a crop blight. Despite this, there have been attempts to promote its culinary use. In the mid-1990s, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) permitted farms in Pennsylvania and Florida to intentionally infect corn with huitlacoche to meet the demand from high-end restaurants. However, this initiative has had limited success. Notably, in 1989, the James Beard Foundation hosted a high-profile dinner featuring huitlacoche, branding it as the Mexican truffle in an effort to make it more appealing to American consumers. Huitlacoche thrives in conditions of drought and temperatures ranging from 78°F to 93°F (25°C to 34°C). Historically, the Aztecs deliberately inoculated corn plants with the fungus by scratching the plants at the soil level, facilitating the entry of waterborne spores. The life cycle of Ustilago maydis begins with its yeast-like growth phase when cultured in simple laboratory media. In this phase, the fungus forms single cells called sporidia, which reproduce by budding. When two compatible sporidia encounter each other on the surface of a maize plant, they undergo a morphological change. They extend conjugation tubes to fuse, forming a dikaryotic hypha that penetrates the plant tissue. These dikaryotic hyphae, which contain two haploid nuclei per compartment, require the host plant for growth and differentiation, as they cannot be sustained in laboratory conditions. Once inside the plant, the fungus proliferates, causing symptoms such as chlorosis, anthocyanin production, stunted growth, and the formation of tumors that house developing teliospores. Mature spores are eventually released from the tumors and dispersed by rain or wind. Under favorable conditions, these spores germinate to form a probasidium, where meiosis occurs. The resulting haploid nuclei migrate into elongated single cells, which detach as sporidia, completing the fungal life cycle. Corn smut has also been used for medicinal purposes. Native American tribes, such as the Zuni, have utilized it to induce labor. Its effects are similar to those of ergot, though weaker, due to the presence of the chemical compound ustilagine. In addition to its culinary and medicinal uses, Ustilago maydis serves as a valuable model organism for scientific research. Its yeast-like growth phase is advantageous for laboratory studies, although its relevance in natural settings remains unclear. The fungus is highly amenable to genetic modification, enabling researchers to investigate host-pathogen interactions with relative ease. The availability of its complete genome further enhances its utility as a model system. Research using Ustilago maydis has contributed to our understanding of plant diseases, DNA recombination, DNA repair, and the role of the cytoskeleton in polarized growth. Notably, studies on this fungus have been instrumental in elucidating the function of the BRCA2 gene, which is associated with breast cancer. Huitlacoche is available for purchase in some markets, often in canned form, and can also be ordered online. Efforts are being made by farmers' markets and organic growers to provide fresh huitlacoche to consumers and local food service industries. For example, the Troy Community Farm in Madison, Wisconsin, initiated a project in 2003 to grow corn infected with huitlacoche. The farm now sells it directly to the public from their weekly farm stand.
